opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the honest starting point is that if your whole business is "we have a slightly better general-purpose model," that's a tough place to be. The frontier labs are spending enormous amounts on compute and research, and whatever edge you have on raw capability tends to get absorbed into the next model release. So I'd steer away from competing on the model itself, unless you have a really distinctive angle on the research.

Where I think startups can compete well is everything around the model. The labs are building a horizontal capability: intelligence you can call through an API. Turning that into something that actually solves a specific problem for a specific customer takes a lot of work. You have to understand the workflow, integrate with the messy systems people already use, handle the edge cases, build trust with the users, and figure out what "good" even means in that domain. That's very hard for a frontier lab to do across thousands of verticals at once, and it's where a focused team can build something durable.

One test I like is to ask whether your product gets better or worse when the next model comes out. If a smarter model makes your product more valuable, because you're the layer that turns that intelligence into outcomes for, say, legal teams or a particular kind of engineer, you're in great shape. You're riding the wave. If a smarter model makes your product unnecessary, because you were mostly patching around the current model's weaknesses with clever prompting or scaffolding, that's the risky zone.

The other area is proprietary data and feedback loops. If being deployed in a domain gives you data the labs can't easily get, like real interactions, expert corrections, and outcomes, you can build a flywheel that compounds over time. Combine that with deep domain knowledge and a real distribution advantage, and I think startups can be very well positioned, even as the underlying models keep getting dramatically better.

r001.rationale: The response says startups can compete by applying models to specific customer problems, requiring deep understanding of domain workflows, existing systems, and edge cases.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that the frontier labs are going to keep pushing on the thing they're uniquely positioned to do, which is make the base model smarter. That's an enormously capital-intensive game. It requires compute, it requires talent, it requires a lot of patience, and it's really not a place where a startup should try to go head to head. If your whole value proposition is "our model is a little better than theirs," you're betting against a team with ten or a hundred times your resources, and the next release can erase your advantage overnight.

But I think the mistake people make is assuming that because the labs own the model, they own everything that sits on top of it. And that's just not true. The labs are, by necessity, building horizontal products. They're trying to serve everyone. And whenever you build for everyone, you leave a tremendous amount of value on the table for people who are willing to go deep on one thing.

So where do I think startups are safe? A few places. The first is anywhere that requires real domain knowledge and real integration into how a specific kind of customer works. If you're building for lawyers, or for radiologists, or for a particular kind of industrial process, the hard part isn't the model. The hard part is understanding the workflow, getting the data in and out, handling the edge cases, earning trust with a buyer who has very specific requirements. The labs aren't going to do that for a thousand different verticals.

The second is anywhere the data is proprietary or hard to get. If you have a relationship with customers that gives you access to data the labs will never see, you can build something that's genuinely better for that use case, even on top of a commodity model. And that advantage compounds over time, because the product gets better the more it's used.

The third, and I think this one's underrated, is the whole layer of orchestration and reliability. Taking a model that's right eighty or ninety percent of the time and turning it into a system that an enterprise will actually depend on is really hard engineering. It's evaluation, it's guardrails, it's knowing when to hand off to a human. That's product work, and it's a place where startups historically have been much better than big platform companies.

The thing I'd caution against is building something that's basically a thin wrapper that just exposes a capability the model already has. That's the zone where you're most likely to get run over, because the lab can ship that as a feature in a week. The test I'd apply is: if the frontier model gets twice as good tomorrow, does my business get better or worse? If the answer is better, because a smarter model makes your product more valuable and you still own the customer and the workflow, you're in a good spot. If the answer is worse, because the model's improvement makes you unnecessary, that's a sign you're competing with the lab whether you meant to or not.

r001.rationale: The response identifies domain-specific customer workflows, integration, edge cases, and trust as areas where deep expertise beyond the model gives startups room to compete.

astra-6.text:
I’d be careful about the word “safely.” If your product is mostly compensating for something the models can’t quite do yet, then a better model can erase a lot of your value. You want to be building something that gets more valuable as the models improve.

I think a lot of that opportunity is in understanding a particular customer and owning the workflow. The model is one component, but you also need integrations, a way to evaluate whether the work was done correctly, and a product people trust enough to use. A frontier lab making a better model doesn’t automatically solve all of those problems.

So I’d ask: if the model got dramatically better tomorrow, would our customers want our product more? If the answer is yes, that’s a much stronger place to build.

r001.rationale: The response identifies deep understanding of a particular customer and owning their workflow, including integrations, evaluation, and trust, as opportunities that remain valuable as models improve.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the strongest place to compete is around a customer problem you understand really well. If your product is essentially a capability the next model release is likely to deliver, that’s a pretty precarious position. But if you understand a particular workflow, have relationships with customers, and can actually get the system deployed and working inside their business, there’s a lot to build there.

The question I’d ask is: If the models get dramatically better, does that make your company more valuable? You want better models to let you solve more of your customer’s problem. You don’t want your business to depend on the models staying bad at something.

r001.rationale: It identifies customer-specific workflows, relationships, and deployment inside a business as places to compete, grounding the advantage in understanding customer problems beyond the model itself.
